title: How to estimate your 1RM without maxing out
description: One hard set of a few reps can estimate your one-rep max, no max attempt needed. How to do it, where it misleads, and how to track it.
imageAlt: Abstract rising steps in Gymon's blue-grey, a placeholder image for this sample article
bottomLine: One hard set of a few reps can replace a max test, if you read the result as an estimate.

cards.label: The idea
cards.heading: A normal hard set already holds the answer
cards.text: Testing a true one-rep max takes a long warm-up, a spotter and a fair bit of nerve. A formula gets you close from a set you were going to do anyway [[r2]]. You put in the weight and the reps, and an estimated max comes out the other end.

cards.label: The catch
cards.heading: The same formula doesn't fit everyone
cards.text: Research suggests that people who are used to long sets squeeze out more reps at the same load [[r1]]. In one small study, endurance runners did about twice as many reps as weightlifters at 70% of their max [[r1]]. So if you estimate from a light, long set, the number can flatter you by a fair margin.

cards.label: Sweet spot
cards.heading: Heavier sets give steadier estimates
cards.text: The gap between the two groups closed as the weight got heavier [[r1]]. That makes a heavy set of a few reps a lot more trustworthy than a long set of fifteen. Pick a weight that feels genuinely heavy, but one you can still move with clean form.

cards.label: Which formula
cards.heading: Epley and Brzycki tell a similar story
cards.text: Both formulas turn your reps into an estimated max, and the calculator below shows them side by side. Epley's version began as a coaching chart rather than a study [[r1]]. That is one more reason to read the result as a rough guide, not a precise figure.

cards.label: What it is for
cards.heading: It works best as a trend line
cards.text: A single estimate on its own says very little, because a good or bad day can move it. The same lift, done the same way week after week, shows whether your strength is moving. That holds even when no single number is exactly right.

steps.title: Pick a lift you know well
steps.text: Choose one you already do every week with steady form, like a squat, bench press or row.

steps.title: Warm up, then do one hard set
steps.text: Use a weight you can lift only a few times, and stop before your form starts to break.

steps.title: Enter the weight and reps
steps.text: Put them into the calculator below and write down the estimate it gives you, with the date.

steps.title: Keep the set the same
steps.text: Same lift, same depth, same rest before it, so next time is a fair comparison.

steps.title: Compare over weeks
steps.text: A rising estimate means you are getting stronger, even in weeks when the bar barely moves.

steps.title: Retest every few weeks
steps.text: Use the estimate as a check-in, not a workout goal, and keep most of your sets well short of failure.

gymon.caption: Two runs of the same bench workout, a week apart. PREVIOUS shows last session's numbers next to each set.
gymon.text: Week 1's best set, 60 kg for 8, gives an Epley estimate of 76 kg. Week 2's, 62.5 kg for 7, gives 77 kg. The weight went up and the reps dipped, so the log alone looks flat. The estimate shows that strength still moved.

references.title: The relationship between the number of repetitions performed at given intensities is different in endurance and strength trained athletes
references.quote: Eight weightlifters and eight endurance runners each completed a one repetition maximum test on the leg press and completed repetitions to fatigue at 90, 80 and 70% of their one repetition maximum. The endurance runners completed significantly more repetitions than the weightlifters at 70% (39.9 ± 17.6 versus 17.9 ± 2.8; p < 0.05) and 80% (19.8 ± 6.4 versus 11.8 ± 2.7; p < 0.05) of their one repetition maximum but not at 90% (10.8 ± 3.9 versus 7.0 ± 2.1; p > 0.05) of one repetition maximum. … Epley [ 8 ] A poundage chart, not based on scientific research.
references.finding: Eight weightlifters and eight endurance runners lifted to failure at 70%, 80% and 90% of their leg-press max. Runners did far more reps at 70% (39.9 vs 17.9) and at 80%, but not at 90%.

references.title: Strength Testing—Predicting a One-Rep Max from Reps-to-Fatigue
references.venue: Journal of Physical Education, Recreation & Dance 64(1):88–90
references.quote: Strength Testing—Predicting a One-Rep Max from Reps-to-Fatigue
references.finding: The 1993 paper that introduced Brzycki's formula for predicting a one-rep max from reps to fatigue. Only the title and listing were read, not the full text.
